steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the "Uses of AI in government" section of an encyclopedia article on artificial intelligence in government: the kinds of problems AI suits, and examples grouped into public policy, helping the public deal with government, gerrymandering, and other uses.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Overview: wide range of uses; Deloitte and Mehr; Mehr's six problem types
- Three broad categories of uses
### Contributing to public policy objectives
### Assisting public interactions with government
### Gerrymandering
### Other uses

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Overview
  - uses wide and varied; Deloitte quote [quote: "Cognitive technologies could eventually revolutionize..."]
  - Mehr: six problem types — resource allocation; large datasets; expert shortage; predictable scenario; procedural tasks (binary answers); diverse data (visual, linguistic; summarized regularly)
  - Mehr quote [quote: AI in government hasn't kept pace with private sector, but use cases mirror it]
- Three categories: public policy objectives, public interactions with government, other
### Contributing to public policy objectives
- benefits at job loss, retirement, bereavement, child birth, automated, no action from citizens
- social insurance service provision
- classifying emergency calls by urgency (Cincinnati Fire Department, United States)
- detecting/preventing spread of diseases
- welfare payments and immigration decisions; bail hearings; triaging health care cases
- social media: public feedback on policies, emergency situations
- fraudulent benefits claims; predicting crime + police presence; traffic congestion and car accidents; road maintenance; health regulation breaches
- personalised education; marking exam papers; defence and national security
- China: 2019, Shanghai government, 100 billion yuan, enterprises using AI, 22 new policy agendas; attract international talent -> Shanghai Municipal Big Data Center
- City Brain AI (Alibaba), urban management platform; capital investment via public and state owned enterprises; public/private synergy beyond capital; provincial and sub-provincial governments control direction
### Assisting public interactions with government
- virtual assistants/chatbots; directing requests within government; filling out forms; searching documents (IP Australia trade mark search); scheduling appointments
- virtual assistants in Australia and Estonia: tax inquiries to life-event registrations
### Gerrymandering
- drawing map boundaries to favor incumbent parties
- Wendy Tam Cho and Bruce Cain: partially automate map-drawing with AI
- can still be manipulated -> transparency and human involvement
### Other uses
- translation
- language interpretation: European Commission's Directorate General for Interpretation, Florika Fink-Hooijer
- drafting documents

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
There are a lot of different potential uses of AI in government. Deloitte considers that "Cognitive technologies could eventually revolutionize every facet of government operations". Mehr suggests that there are six types of government problems that are appropriate for AI applications:

Resource allocation, for example where administrative support is needed to get tasks done more quickly.

Large datasets, where they are too large for employees to work with efficiently and multiple datasets could be combined to give greater insights.

Expert shortage, including where basic questions could be answered and niche issues can be learned.

Predictable scenario, where the historical data makes the situation predictable.

Procedural tasks, which are repetitive tasks where the answers to inputs or outputs are binary.

Diverse data, where the data takes various forms (such as visual and linguistic) and has to be summarized regularly.

Mehr says that "While applications of AI in government work have not kept pace with the rapid expansion of AI in the private sector, the potential use cases in the public sector mirror common applications in the private sector."

The potential and actual uses of AI in government can be split into three broad categories: uses that contribute to public policy objectives, uses that help the public interact with the government, and other uses.

### Contributing to public policy objectives

There are a range of examples where AI can contribute to public policy objectives. They include:

Receiving benefits almost immediately at job loss, retirement, bereavement and child birth, in an automated way, so citizens don't need to take any actions at all

Providing social insurance services

Classifying emergency calls by how urgent they are (like the system the Cincinnati Fire Department uses in the United States)

Detecting diseases and preventing them from spreading

Helping public servants make welfare payments and immigration decisions

Adjudicating bail hearings

Triaging health care cases

Monitoring social media for public feedback on policies

Monitoring social media to identify emergency situations

Identifying fraudulent benefits claims

Predicting a crime and recommending the optimal police presence

Predicting traffic congestion and car accidents

Anticipating road maintenance requirements

Identifying breaches of health regulations

Providing personalised education to students

Marking exam papers

Assisting with defence and national security

China:
- 2019, Shanghai government, 100 billion yuan for enterprises using AI, 22 new policy agendas
- attract top international talent, set up Shanghai Municipal Big Data Center
- City Brain AI (Alibaba), urban management platform; capital investment through public and state owned enterprises
- public/private synergy more than capital-driven; provincial and sub-provincial governments control its direction

### Assisting public interactions with government
- virtual assistants/chatbots; directing requests; filling out forms; searching documents (IP Australia trade mark search); scheduling appointments
- Australia, Estonia virtual assistants: tax inquiries to life-event registrations

### Gerrymandering
- definition: map boundaries drawn to favor incumbent parties
- Wendy Tam Cho and Bruce Cain: partially automate map-drawing with AI
- still manipulable -> transparency, human involvement

### Other uses
- translation; language interpretation (European Commission's Directorate General for Interpretation, Florika Fink-Hooijer); drafting documents

steps.text:
There are a lot of different potential uses of AI in government. Deloitte considers that "Cognitive technologies could eventually revolutionize every facet of government operations". Mehr suggests that there are six types of government problems that are appropriate for AI applications:

Resource allocation, for example where administrative support is needed to get tasks done more quickly.

Large datasets, where they are too large for employees to work with efficiently and multiple datasets could be combined to give greater insights.

Expert shortage, including where basic questions could be answered and niche issues can be learned.

Predictable scenario, where the historical data makes the situation predictable.

Procedural tasks, which are repetitive tasks where the answers to inputs or outputs are binary.

Diverse data, where the data takes various forms (such as visual and linguistic) and has to be summarized regularly.

Mehr says that "While applications of AI in government work have not kept pace with the rapid expansion of AI in the private sector, the potential use cases in the public sector mirror common applications in the private sector."

The potential and actual uses of AI in government can be split into three broad categories: uses that contribute to public policy objectives, uses that help the public interact with the government, and other uses.

### Contributing to public policy objectives

There are a range of examples where AI can contribute to public policy objectives. They include:

Receiving benefits almost immediately at job loss, retirement, bereavement and child birth, in an automated way, so citizens don't need to take any actions at all

Providing social insurance services

Classifying emergency calls by how urgent they are (like the system the Cincinnati Fire Department uses in the United States)

Detecting diseases and preventing them from spreading

Helping public servants make welfare payments and immigration decisions

Adjudicating bail hearings

Triaging health care cases

Monitoring social media for public feedback on policies

Monitoring social media to identify emergency situations

Identifying fraudulent benefits claims

Predicting a crime and recommending the optimal police presence

Predicting traffic congestion and car accidents

Anticipating road maintenance requirements

Identifying breaches of health regulations

Providing personalised education to students

Marking exam papers

Assisting with defence and national security

In China, Artificial Intelligence has been used to drive both political and economic markets. In 2019 Shanghai's government rolled out 100 billion yuan to help fund enterprises that used AI, to introduce 22 new policy agendas. Shanghai invested in these enterprises to attract top international talent so it could set up the Shanghai Municipal Big Data Center. City Brain AI is an urban management platform that Alibaba made. China uses City Brain AI to keep a significant share of capital investment through public and state owned enterprises. With City Brain AI the synergy between the public and private sectors is more than just capital-driven. The blend of public and private shareholding is only made out to be through the role of the provincial and sub-provincial governments. Both of them hold control over the direction City Brain AI takes, socially and economically.

### Assisting public interactions with government

AI can be used to help members of the public interact with government and access government services, for example by:

Answering questions with virtual assistants or chatbots

Directing requests to the right area within government

Filling out forms

Helping with searching documents (e.g. IP Australia's trade mark search)

Scheduling appointments

Various governments have implemented virtual assistants to help citizens navigate services, including Australia and Estonia, and the applications range from tax inquiries to life-event registrations.

### Gerrymandering

Gerrymandering is when map boundaries are drawn in favor of incumbent parties, as a way of influencing the political process. The academic researchers Wendy Tam Cho and Bruce Cain have proposed using an AI system to partially automate drawing the maps, to reduce partisan gerrymandering. But even with the AI system the process could still be manipulated to favor partisan interests, so the researchers emphasized that transparency and human involvement are important.

### Other uses

Other uses of AI in government are:

Translation

Language interpretation, pioneered by the European Commission's Directorate General for Interpretation and Florika Fink-Hooijer.

Drafting documents

steps.text:
The potential uses of AI in government are wide and varied,[1] with Deloitte considering that "Cognitive technologies could eventually revolutionize every facet of government operations".[2] Mehr suggests that six types of government problems are appropriate for AI applications:[3]

Resource allocation—such as where administrative support is needed to complete tasks more quickly.

Large datasets—where these are too large for employees to work with efficiently and multiple datasets could be combined to provide greater insights.

Expert shortage—including where basic questions could be answered and niche issues can be learned.

Predictable scenario—historical data makes the situation predictable.

Procedural tasks—repetitive tasks in which the answers to inputs or outputs are binary.

Diverse data—where data takes various forms (such as visual and linguistic) and needs to be summarized regularly.

Mehr states that "While applications of AI in government work have not kept pace with the rapid expansion of AI in the private sector, the potential use cases in the public sector mirror common applications in the private sector."[3]

Potential and actual uses of AI in government can be divided into three broad categories: those that contribute to public policy objectives, those that assist public interactions with the government, and other uses.

### Contributing to public policy objectives

There are a range of examples of where AI can contribute to public policy objectives.[1] These include:

Receiving benefits at job loss, retirement, bereavement and child birth almost immediately, in an automated way (without requiring any actions from citizens)[4]

Social insurance service provision[5]

Classifying emergency calls based on their urgency (like the system used by the Cincinnati Fire Department in the United States[6])

Detecting and preventing the spread of diseases[6]

Assisting public servants in making welfare payments and immigration decisions[7]

Adjudicating bail hearings[7]

Triaging health care cases[7]

Monitoring social media for public feedback on policies[8]

Monitoring social media to identify emergency situations[8]

Identifying fraudulent benefits claims[8]

Predicting a crime and recommending optimal police presence[8]

Predicting traffic congestion and car accidents[8]

Anticipating road maintenance requirements[8]

Identifying breaches of health regulations[8]

Providing personalised education to students[6]

Marking exam papers[7]

Assisting with defence and national security

Artificial Intelligence in China has been used to drive both political and economic markets. In 2019, Shanghai's government rolled out 100 billion yuan to help fund enterprises that used AI to introduce 22 new policy agendas. Shanghai invested in these enterprises to attract top international talent in order to set up the Shanghai Municipal Big Data Center. City Brain AI is an urban management platform made by Alibaba, which China uses to maintain a significant share of capital investment through public and state owned enterprises. The synergy between public and private sectors with City Brain AI is more than capital-driven. The blend of public and private shareholding is only made out to be through the role of provincial and sub-provincial governments, both of which hold control over the direction City Brain AI takes socially and economically.[9]

### Assisting public interactions with government

AI can be used to assist members of the public to interact with government and access government services,[1] for example by:

Answering questions using virtual assistants or chatbots

Directing requests to the appropriate area within government[3]

Filling out forms[3]

Assisting with searching documents (e.g. IP Australia's trade mark search[10])

Scheduling appointments[8]

Various governments, including those of Australia[11] and Estonia,[12] have implemented virtual assistants to help citizens navigate services, with applications ranging from tax inquiries to life-event registrations.

### Gerrymandering

Gerrymandering is a method of influencing the political process by drawing map boundaries in favor of incumbent parties. Academic researchers Wendy Tam Cho and Bruce Cain have proposed partially automating the map-drawing process with an AI system in order to reduce partisan gerrymandering. Since the process may still be manipulated to favor partisan interests even with this AI system, the researchers emphasized the importance of transparency and human involvement.[13,14]

### Other uses

Other uses of AI in government include:

Translation[3]

Language interpretation pioneered by the European Commission's Directorate General for Interpretation and Florika Fink-Hooijer.

Drafting documents[3]
